description.summary: Ancient Egyptian jackal-headed deity associated with mummification, the protection of tombs, and the conduct of souls through the underworld; one of the longest-lived figures in Egyptian religion.
description.full: Anubis (Egyptian Inpw / Anpu) is an ancient Egyptian deity associated with mummification, the protection of cemeteries, and the journey of the dead through the underworld. He is consistently depicted either as a man with the head of a black jackal-like canid or in full canid form. The black colour of his coat is symbolic rather than zoological, evoking both the discoloration of the body during natron desiccation and the fertile black silt of the Nile from which new life rises. Anubis was worshipped from the Predynastic period (c. 4000 BCE) into the Roman era and was the principal funerary god of the Old Kingdom; in the Middle Kingdom Osiris rose in prominence and Anubis took on a constellation of subordinate but enduring roles, including 'He who is upon his mountain' (guardian of the cemetery), 'He who is in the place of embalming', 'Lord of the Sacred Land', and 'Opener of the Ways'. In the iconic judgment scene of Chapter 125 of the Book of the Dead, Anubis presides over the weighing of the heart against the feather of Maat. His parents and children differ across traditions: he is variously the son of Ra, of Set and Nephthys, or (in later tradition) of Osiris and Nephthys, and is the father of the serpent goddess Kebechet. In the Ptolemaic and Roman periods Anubis was syncretised with the Greek Hermes as Hermanubis. His main cult centre was at Hardai, called by the Greeks Cynopolis ('city of the dog').

etymology.origin: Anubis is the Greek rendering of the Egyptian Inpw / Anpu.
etymology.meaning: The name's root has been connected to the word 'inp' associated with decay, fitting his funerary role; alternative folk-etymologies relate it to 'a royal child'.
etymology.first_use: Anubis is attested from the Old Kingdom (c. 2700 BCE) and possibly earlier in Predynastic iconography of canids on cemetery standards.

related_phenomena.name: Wepwawet
related_phenomena.description: Other Egyptian canid deity, 'Opener of the Ways'

related_phenomena.name: Hermanubis
related_phenomena.description: Greco-Egyptian syncretism of Anubis and Hermes

features.description: Head of a black jackal-like canid (debated as jackal, dog, or fox-jackal hybrid)
Symbolic black coat evoking mummification and fertile Nile soil
Most often depicted as a man with the canid head; full canid form also frequent
Frequently depicted holding the was-sceptre and ankh, attributes of divine authority and life

physical.morphology: Standard Egyptian zoocephalic deity form: human body with the head of a black canid.

abilities.description: Patron and divine performer of mummification rites
Guides the deceased through the underworld and the judgment scene
Operates the scales in the judgment of the dead against the feather of Maat
Guards cemeteries from desecration as 'He who is upon his mountain'

range.description: Worshipped throughout ancient Egypt, with principal cult centre at Hardai (Cynopolis) in Upper Egypt; cult spread into the wider Greco-Roman world during the Ptolemaic and Roman periods.

hotspots.name: Cynopolis (Hardai)

location.description: Anubis's principal cult centre in the 17th Upper Egyptian nome

hotspots.notes: Greek 'Cynopolis' translates 'city of the dog'; major centre of canid mummification.

hotspots.name: Anubieion at Saqqara

location.description: Temple complex of Anubis at the Saqqara necropolis

hotspots.notes: Site of large-scale canid catacombs and pilgrim activity.

peak_activity_periods.description: Anubis is the principal funerary god
Standardised judgment iconography of the Book of the Dead

origins.cultural_roots: Egyptian Predynastic and Old Kingdom funerary religion, observing the role of canids around cemetery margins.
origins.earliest_accounts: Old Kingdom mortuary inscriptions naming Inpw / Anpu; Predynastic standards bearing canids may anticipate the figure.
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to the broader Egyptian family of canid deities (Wepwawet, Khentiamentiu) and to the Greco-Roman Hermanubis.

timeline.event: Anubis attested as principal funerary god in Old Kingdom mortuary inscriptions
timeline.significance: Establishes him at the head of the funerary pantheon
timeline.source: Pyramid Texts and Old Kingdom mastaba inscriptions

timeline.event: Rise of Osiris partially supplants Anubis as lord of the underworld in the Middle Kingdom
Anubis depicted presiding over the Weighing of the Heart in New Kingdom Books of the Dead
timeline.significance: Iconic image of Anubis enters its canonical form
timeline.source: Book of the Dead corpus (e.g. Papyrus of Ani, Papyrus of Hunefer)

timeline.event: Ptolemaic and Roman-era syncretism produces Hermanubis
timeline.significance: Anubis enters the wider Mediterranean religious world

history.modern_era: Anubis is one of the most globally recognised figures of Egyptian religion, central to museum collections worldwide and to popular representations of ancient Egypt in literature, film, and games.

physical.name: Anubis Shrine of Tutankhamun
physical.description: Wooden recumbent Anubis figure on a portable shrine, recovered from the tomb of Tutankhamun (KV62) by Howard Carter in 1922.
physical.location: Egyptian Museum, Cairo / Grand Egyptian Museum

documentary.name: Papyrus of Ani — judgment scene
documentary.description: 19th Dynasty Book of the Dead papyrus depicting Anubis conducting the weighing of the heart.

scientific.name: Funerary deity rooted in observation of canids
scientific.description: Egyptologists understand the figure as an Old Kingdom funerary deity whose canid form reflects the historical role of jackals and feral dogs as observers and scavengers at cemeteries on the desert margin.
evidence_cited: Cemetery topography on the desert margin
Continuity of canid imagery through Egyptian religion

traditions: New Kingdom Book of the Dead tradition
stories: The judgment of the dead before Osiris (Book of the Dead, Chapter 125)
The mummification of Osiris by Anubis (Plutarch, On Isis and Osiris)
folklore.beliefs: Anubis embodied the careful, ritualised relationship between Egyptian society and its dead.

literature: The Egyptian Book of the Dead — translated by R. O. Faulkner (1972)
film_tv: Stargate (1994) and Stargate SG-1 — fictional depiction
other: Anubis statuary in the British Museum, the Louvre, and the Egyptian Museum, Cairo
